title: Chocolate for a Hangover: Does It Help and Why You Crave It
excerpt: Does chocolate help a hangover? Why alcohol and poor sleep trigger chocolate cravings, whether dark or milk chocolate is better, chocolate milk and hot cocoa, and when to skip it.
metaDescription: Does chocolate help a hangover? Why you crave it, dark vs milk chocolate, chocolate milk, caffeine content, and when chocolate makes a hangover worse.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** chocolate won't cure a hangover, and there is no good evidence that it speeds up recovery. But a small amount of dark chocolate isn't a bad choice either. It gives you a little sugar for low energy, some magnesium and potassium, and a gentle dose of caffeine and theobromine that can take the edge off the morning fog. The intense craving you feel for it is real and has a clear explanation: alcohol and a short night of sleep both push your brain toward fast, sweet, calorie-dense food. The trick is to treat chocolate as a side, not the meal, and to skip it if your stomach is queasy or you have heartburn.

**The quick rules:** Pick dark chocolate (70% cocoa or more) over milk chocolate or candy bars. Keep it to a square or two (about an ounce). Eat it alongside real food and plenty of water, not instead of them. If you feel sick to your stomach or have acid reflux after drinking, leave the chocolate for later in the day. And if you're looking for something that actually helps, focus on fluids, a proper meal, and sleep first.

> **When to see a doctor.** A normal hangover is miserable but passes within about a day. **Get medical help if** you can't keep any fluids down for several hours, you're vomiting repeatedly or see blood, you feel confused, very drowsy, or faint, your heart is racing or beating irregularly and doesn't settle, you have severe stomach pain, or your symptoms are getting worse after 24 hours instead of better. If you have diabetes and drank alcohol, watch closely for signs of low blood sugar such as shakiness, sweating, and confusion, and follow your care plan. If someone can't be woken, is breathing very slowly, or is having a seizure, call 911. Shaking, sweating, and anxiety that show up when you stop drinking after many days of heavy drinking can be alcohol withdrawal, which needs a doctor, not a snack.

## Does Chocolate Help a Hangover?

Short version: it can make you feel a bit better, but it isn't treating the hangover itself.

A hangover is a mix of several things happening at once. Your sleep was poor. You're likely somewhat dehydrated. Your immune system is reacting to the alcohol with a low-grade inflammatory response. Your stomach lining is irritated. And your body has been busy breaking down alcohol into acetaldehyde, a toxic by-product, and then clearing it. Researchers who study hangovers, including the Alcohol Hangover Research Group, have pointed out that no single cause explains all the symptoms, which is also why no single food fixes them.

Chocolate touches a few of those pieces, lightly:

- **Energy.** The sugar in chocolate gives you quick fuel when you feel drained.
- **Alertness.** Cocoa naturally contains caffeine and a related compound called theobromine. Both are mild stimulants.
- **Minerals.** Dark chocolate has a surprising amount of magnesium and some potassium, two minerals that drinking can lower.
- **Mood.** Eating something you enjoy when you feel rough is a real comfort, even if it's not a medical effect.

What it doesn't do: it won't rehydrate you, it won't clear alcohol faster, and it won't settle an upset stomach. There are no clinical studies that test chocolate as a hangover remedy, so anyone telling you it's a proven fix is overselling it.

## Why You Crave Chocolate When You're Hungover

If you've ever woken up after a night out and wanted nothing more than a chocolate bar, a pastry, or a stack of pancakes, you're not weak-willed. Several things are pushing you in that direction at the same time.

### Alcohol switches on hunger signals

Alcohol stimulates appetite. Studies in people have long shown that drinking alcohol before or with a meal leads people to eat more than they otherwise would, sometimes called the "apéritif effect." Animal research has gone a step further. A 2017 study in *Nature Communications* from researchers at the Francis Crick Institute found that alcohol activated a group of hunger-driving brain cells (called AgRP neurons) in mice, and that blocking those cells reduced the overeating. Mouse findings don't translate neatly to people, but they fit with what most drinkers already know: alcohol makes you hungry, and that hunger often carries into the next morning.

### Poor sleep raises your appetite for sweet, fast calories

Alcohol might help you fall asleep, but it breaks up your sleep later in the night, especially the deeper and dream-rich stages. Short or broken sleep changes your appetite hormones. A well-known 2004 study in the *Annals of Internal Medicine* found that when healthy young men slept only four hours a night for two nights, their levels of ghrelin (a hormone that drives hunger) went up, their levels of leptin (a hormone that signals fullness) went down, and they reported more hunger, especially for carbohydrate-rich foods like sweets and starchy snacks. A hangover morning often looks a lot like that experiment.

### Your blood sugar may have dipped

When your liver is busy processing alcohol, it's less able to make new glucose and release it into your blood. In people who drank heavily without eating much, this can lead to lower blood sugar the next morning. Low blood sugar makes you shaky, irritable, and hungry for something sweet, fast.

It's worth being honest about how much this matters. Researchers have looked at whether low blood sugar explains hangover symptoms, and the link is weak. Blood sugar levels don't track closely with how bad a hangover feels. So the dip is one more nudge toward chocolate, not the main reason you feel awful.

### Chocolate is a comfort food by design

Chocolate combines sugar and fat, has a pleasant melt-in-the-mouth texture, and for most of us comes with a lifetime of good associations. When you feel tired, anxious, and run-down, your brain reaches for reliable rewards. That's not a hangover-specific effect, but it's part of why the craving feels so strong.

### What about serotonin and "feel-good" chemicals?

You'll often read that chocolate boosts serotonin or contains "bliss molecules" that lift your mood. Chocolate does contain small amounts of compounds like tryptophan, phenylethylamine, and anandamide-like substances, but the amounts in a normal serving are tiny, and there's no good evidence that they meaningfully change brain chemistry when you eat a square or two. The mood lift you feel is most likely the simple pleasure of eating something tasty, plus a small caffeine kick.

## What's Actually in Chocolate (and Why It Matters the Morning After)

Not all chocolate is the same. The cocoa percentage changes almost everything about it.

| What it has | Dark chocolate (70-85% cocoa) | Milk chocolate | Why it matters when hungover |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sugar | Lower | Much higher | Too much sugar can leave you crashing again an hour later |
| Caffeine | Moderate (more than milk chocolate) | Low | A mild lift without the jolt of a big coffee |
| Theobromine | Higher | Lower | Gentle stimulant; slower and milder than caffeine |
| Magnesium | Meaningful amount | Small amount | Drinking can lower magnesium |
| Potassium | Some | Less | Helps with fluid balance alongside sodium |
| Fat | High | High | Rich foods can upset a sensitive stomach |

A few specifics, using rough figures that vary by brand:

- **Magnesium.** Based on USDA nutrition data, an ounce (about 28 grams) of 70-85% dark chocolate provides roughly 60 to 65 mg of magnesium. That's around 15% of what most adults need in a day. It's one of the richer common food sources.
- **Potassium.** That same ounce has roughly 200 mg of potassium. A medium banana has about twice that, so chocolate is a supporting player here, not the star.
- **Caffeine.** An ounce of dark chocolate usually has somewhere around 12 to 25 mg of caffeine, compared with roughly 95 mg in an average 8-ounce cup of brewed coffee. Milk chocolate has much less.
- **Calories.** An ounce of dark chocolate is around 170 calories, most of them from fat.

### Theobromine: chocolate's other stimulant

Theobromine is the main stimulant in cocoa, and dark chocolate has far more of it than caffeine. It belongs to the same chemical family as caffeine but acts more gently and lasts longer. People often describe the effect as a mild, steady lift rather than a buzz. It also has a mild diuretic effect (it makes you pee a little more), though the amount in a few squares of chocolate is small. There's no research on theobromine for hangovers specifically, so treat any "theobromine fixes hangovers" claim with suspicion.

### Flavanols: interesting, but not a hangover fix

Cocoa is rich in plant compounds called flavanols. These have been studied mostly for heart and blood vessel health, with some promising results in research using concentrated cocoa extracts. That research doesn't tell us anything about hangovers. A typical chocolate bar also contains far less of these compounds than the extracts used in studies, especially once cocoa has been heavily processed or "Dutched." It's fine to see flavanols as a small bonus. It's not a reason to eat more chocolate.

## Dark Chocolate vs Milk Chocolate for a Hangover

If you're going to have chocolate, dark is the better pick for three reasons.

1. **Less sugar.** A hangover morning is already a recipe for an energy rollercoaster. A sugar-heavy candy bar can give you a quick rise followed by a slump. Dark chocolate has less sugar and more fat and fiber, so it hits more gently.
2. **More minerals.** You get noticeably more magnesium, iron, and potassium per bite.
3. **Easier to stop at a little.** Dark chocolate is richer and less sweet, so most people feel satisfied with a smaller amount.

Milk chocolate and candy bars aren't harmful in a normal portion. They're just mostly sugar and fat, and they bring very little else to the table. Chocolate bars packed with caramel, nougat, or cookie pieces are effectively dessert.

One caution in the other direction: very dark chocolate (85% and up) has the most caffeine and the most bitterness. If your stomach is unsettled or you're already jittery, it may not feel great.

## Chocolate Milk and Hot Chocolate After Drinking

Drinking your chocolate is a different story from eating a bar, mostly because it brings fluid with it.

**Chocolate milk** gives you water, carbohydrates, protein, and some sodium and potassium. Sports researchers have studied low-fat chocolate milk as a recovery drink after exercise, with generally favorable results for replacing fluids and fuel. That's not the same as hangover research, and no study has tested it for hangovers, but the basic idea that it combines fluid, sugar, and protein holds. The downside is that dairy can feel heavy if your stomach is upset. For a closer look at dairy the morning after, see our guide on [whether milk helps a hangover](/never-hungover/milk-for-hangover).

**Hot chocolate** is mainly comforting. A warm drink in your hands can be soothing when you feel rough, and the cocoa gives a mild lift. Made with water or milk, it also counts toward your fluid intake. Packet mixes are often very sweet, so a homemade version with real cocoa powder and a little sugar is the better choice if you have the energy.

Neither one replaces plain water or an electrolyte drink if you're properly dehydrated. Think of them as a nice addition once you've had a couple of glasses of water.

## When Chocolate Can Make a Hangover Worse

Chocolate is mostly harmless, but there are a few situations where it's a poor choice.

### If you have heartburn or acid reflux

Chocolate is one of the foods most often linked with heartburn. It can relax the ring of muscle at the bottom of your esophagus (the tube that carries food to your stomach), which makes it easier for stomach acid to splash upward. Alcohol does the same thing and also irritates the stomach lining. Put the two together the morning after, and you can end up with a burning chest and sour taste. If that sounds familiar, our guide to [heartburn after drinking](/never-hungover/heartburn-after-drinking) covers what helps.

### If you feel nauseous

Fatty, rich foods sit in the stomach longer. When you're queasy, that's the opposite of what you want. Plain toast, crackers, rice, or a banana usually go down more easily. Ginger tea can help, too. Our [hangover nausea guide](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) goes through the gentlest options. Save the chocolate for later in the day, once your stomach has settled.

### If you have diarrhea

Some people find that rich foods, caffeine, and lots of sugar all make an upset gut worse. Chocolate has all three. If drinking has sent you running to the bathroom, stick with bland foods and fluids for a while. See our guide on [diarrhea after drinking](/never-hungover/diarrhea-after-drinking) for more.

### If you get hangover headaches or migraines

Chocolate has a long reputation as a migraine trigger. The evidence for that is actually weak. Some researchers think the craving for chocolate can be an early sign that a migraine is already starting, which makes chocolate look guilty when it isn't. Alcohol, especially red wine, is a better-supported trigger for many migraine sufferers. If you know chocolate bothers you personally, trust your own experience. Otherwise, there's no strong reason to avoid it. For general relief options, see our [hangover headache guide](/never-hungover/hangover-headache-fast-relief-methods-2025).

### If you're jittery or anxious

Chocolate's caffeine dose is small, but if you've already had two coffees and you're feeling the shaky, anxious edge that sometimes comes with a hangover, it adds up. Our page on [hangover shakes](/never-hungover/hangover-shakes) explains where that trembling comes from.

### If you're eating it instead of a meal

This is the most common problem. A chocolate bar for breakfast gives you a short burst of energy with no protein, little fiber, and almost no fluid. You'll likely feel hungry and drained again soon. Chocolate works best as a small extra after real food.

## How to Use Chocolate Sensibly the Morning After

If chocolate is what you want, here's a reasonable way to fit it in:

1. **Drink first.** Start with a big glass of water or an electrolyte drink. Fluid is the most reliable thing you can do for how you feel.
2. **Eat a real meal.** Eggs, toast, oatmeal, yogurt, fruit, or a simple sandwich give you protein, carbs, and some salt. Our roundup of the [best foods for a hangover](/never-hungover/best-foods-for-hangover) and our [hangover breakfast guide](/never-hungover/best-hangover-breakfast) have plenty of ideas.
3. **Then have a square or two of dark chocolate.** About an ounce is enough to satisfy the craving and get the small mineral and caffeine benefit.
4. **Pair it with fruit.** Dark chocolate with a banana or some berries adds potassium, fiber, and more fluid. Melted dark chocolate on oatmeal is another easy option.
5. **Watch your total caffeine.** If you're also having coffee, remember that chocolate adds a bit more. Our guide to [coffee for a hangover](/never-hungover/coffee-for-hangover) covers how much is sensible.
6. **Rest.** Sleep does more for a hangover than anything you eat.

### Simple chocolate pairings that work

- **Banana and dark chocolate:** potassium, quick carbs, and something sweet.
- **Oatmeal with a few dark chocolate chips:** slow-release carbs that keep you going longer than chocolate alone.
- **Greek yogurt, berries, and grated dark chocolate:** protein, fluid, and fruit in one bowl.
- **Warm cocoa made with milk:** fluid plus a gentle lift, if your stomach tolerates dairy.
- **Peanut butter on toast with a square of chocolate on the side:** protein and fat to blunt the sugar hit.

## What Actually Helps a Hangover

Since chocolate plays only a supporting role, it's worth knowing what does the heavy lifting.

- **Fluids and electrolytes.** Alcohol makes you pee more, and vomiting or sweating adds to the loss. Water helps, and an electrolyte drink helps more if you've lost a lot.
- **Food.** A balanced meal with some carbohydrate, protein, and salt helps steady your energy and settle your stomach.
- **Sleep.** Alcohol wrecks sleep quality. Extra rest is often the single most effective thing you can do.
- **Time.** Most hangovers fade within about 24 hours. Nothing reliably shortens that dramatically.
- **Pain relief, carefully.** If you need a painkiller, follow the label and be careful with alcohol interactions, especially with acetaminophen (Tylenol) and on an empty stomach with ibuprofen or aspirin.

The best "remedy" is prevention: eating before you drink, pacing yourself, alternating alcoholic drinks with water, and stopping earlier. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence behind them.

## Where DHM Fits In

Some people who drink socially add a supplement called **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree, to their routine. It has been studied for its effects on how the body handles alcohol and for liver health. Most of that research has been done in animals and in the lab, with only a small amount of human data. It's promising, but there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers in everyone, and it isn't a substitute for drinking less, eating, and staying hydrated.

If you want to try it, it's usually taken with water around the time you drink. Popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much people typically take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take prescription medication, check with a pharmacist before adding any supplement.

And yes, you can still have the chocolate.

## The Bottom Line

- Chocolate won't cure a hangover, and no studies have tested it as a remedy.
- The craving is real: alcohol stimulates hunger, poor sleep shifts your appetite toward sweet, fast calories, and your blood sugar may be a bit low.
- Dark chocolate (70% or more) is the better choice. It has less sugar, a useful amount of magnesium, some potassium, and a mild caffeine and theobromine lift.
- Keep it to about an ounce, and eat it after water and a real meal, not instead of them.
- Skip it if you have heartburn, nausea, or an upset gut, and save it for later in the day.
- If symptoms are severe or getting worse after a day, or you can't keep fluids down, see a doctor.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is chocolate good for a hangover?**

It's not a cure, but a small amount of dark chocolate can help you feel a little better. It provides quick energy, some magnesium and potassium, and a mild lift from caffeine and theobromine. It won't rehydrate you or settle your stomach, so have it after water and a proper meal rather than instead of them.

**Why do I crave chocolate when I'm hungover?**

Several reasons stack up. Alcohol stimulates appetite, and short or broken sleep raises the hunger hormone ghrelin and lowers the fullness hormone leptin, which pushes you toward sweet, high-calorie food. Heavy drinking can also lower your blood sugar the next morning. On top of that, chocolate is a familiar comfort food, and your brain reaches for easy rewards when you feel run-down.

**Is dark chocolate or milk chocolate better for a hangover?**

Dark chocolate with 70% cocoa or more is the better choice. It has less sugar, so you're less likely to crash later, and more magnesium, iron, and potassium. It also tends to satisfy you with a smaller portion. Very dark chocolate has the most caffeine, so go easy if you already feel jittery.

**Does chocolate milk help a hangover?**

It can be a reasonable choice if your stomach is fine with dairy. It provides fluid, carbohydrates, protein, and some sodium and potassium. It has been studied as an exercise recovery drink, but not as a hangover remedy. If you're queasy, plain water, an electrolyte drink, or a light broth will usually sit better.

**How much caffeine is in chocolate?**

It varies by brand, but an ounce of dark chocolate usually has roughly 12 to 25 mg of caffeine, while milk chocolate has much less. For comparison, an average cup of brewed coffee has around 95 mg. Chocolate also contains theobromine, a milder, longer-lasting stimulant from the same chemical family.

**Can chocolate make a hangover worse?**

It can in some cases. Chocolate can relax the muscle that keeps stomach acid out of your esophagus, so it may worsen heartburn, which alcohol already encourages. Its fat, sugar, and caffeine can also make nausea or diarrhea worse. If your stomach is upset, choose bland foods first and save the chocolate for later.

**Does chocolate help with hangover headaches?**

There's no good evidence that chocolate relieves hangover headaches. Its small amount of caffeine may help a little if you're used to caffeine and missed your morning dose. Water, rest, food, and an appropriate pain reliever taken according to the label are more reliable.

**Is it bad to eat chocolate before drinking alcohol?**

A little chocolate before drinking isn't harmful, but it's not a good substitute for a proper meal. Food that includes protein, fat, and fiber slows how fast alcohol reaches your bloodstream. A chocolate bar alone is mostly sugar and fat and won't do much to protect you. Eat a real meal first if you plan to drink.
